newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala military police end five-day rebellion.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala military police end five-day rebellion.

text.p: Hundreds of Guatemalan military police ended a tense, five-day rebellion over terms of a peace treaty on Sunday, although regular army troops remained on alert in case of a renewed outbreak of skirmishes.

Troops and armoured vehicles maintained positions around a military police barracks, but the police confirmed they had ended their rebellion. One general who was taken hostage at the barracks on Saturday was released on Sunday morning.
Small tanks roamed around the barracks and soldiers manned a 150-mm cannon trained on the large, grey fortified building. Rebellious military police either went back to work or took the day off.
"Everything has normalised. It's like any weekend here. Some of us went to work and some are at home resting," one military policeman told Reuters.
There was no formal laying down of arms by the military police, although the government had stipulated the unit must turn in their weapons for negotiations to start.

"Our personnel came to a peaceful understanding that the solution to this problem was to turn in their weapons. They will start coming out as civilians and we will restore services," Maj. Julio Cesar Linares of the military police told reporters.

Army troops and tanks had surrounded the barracks on Saturday night as hundreds of disgruntled military police holding the fortified compound demanded government negotiators promise them severance pay when they lose their jobs later this year.
So tense was the stand-off that troops and rebellious military police had a brief exchange of fire late on Saturday. No one was hurt.

The entire 4,000-member military police force will be disbanded this year as part of drastic army cuts the government promised when it signed peace accords on Dec. 29 with leftist rebels the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG).

The army has played a pivotal and at times brutal role in political life for much of Guatemala's recent history. Decades of civil wars claimed an estimated 140,000 lives, including many poor Indian civilians killed in army counterinsurgency campaigns.
The military police rebellion this week marked the first sign of military discontent over terms of the breakthrough peace accord.

Until Saturday, the government had played down the insubordination. A presidential spokesman had called it a "labor dispute." But on Sunday army spokesman Col. Otto Noack said the army had decided the uprising was a criminal act of rebellion.
Military police commander Leonel de Leon Guillen met on Sunday morning with Defence Minister Julio Balconi. Noack said the meeting was informational, not a negotiation.

According to Noack, Balconi told ex-president Ramiro de Leon Carpio, who also intervened to resolve the rebellion, that the government would not negotiate unless the military police turned in their weapons.
Approximately 400 military police, fewer than half of the number housed in the barracks, had refused to turn in their assault rifles and machineguns since Wednesday.
